data.abstractNote: The author's Ph.D. work in Rome first traces the history of the Syro-Malabar Church and with a focus on migratory movements. The second section deals with rites and the different rites acceptable in the Roman Catholic communion in India. data.title: Ο πρώιμος κύκλος των παθών: λόγος, ράζα και συναίσθημα
data.abstractNote: The early Christian Passion cycle is examined through textual analysis as well as through the surviving examples from the 4th c. to the iconoclastic period in order to answer the following: When were the various scenes added to the cycle and why? How did the expression of emotion develop and how was it influenced by the written word? The analysis of texts begins with the earliest written accounts on the Passion from the epistles of Paul and the Gospels to the Gnostic and Orthodox writings of the 2nd c. The shift from the use of symbols and types to realism to explain the nature of the mystery of divine revelation is examined. The central theological issue in the development of the cycle is also discussed, that is, the question of suffering and how Christ’s human nature suffered while His divine nature remained impassible. Finally, the evolution of the formation of Holy Week ritual is traced in order to shed light on the question of whether the emergence of the Passion cycle is linked to this development or whether they are perhaps parallel phenomena. The analysis of the art is prefaced with the attempt to address some fundamental issues, such as the disparity between the literary exploration of the theme of the Passion and its artistic expression. Representation of the Passion was absent among the earliest manifestations of Christian art, thus indicating that this theme was not easily approached. The way in which Byzantines thought of and talked about the Passion is also examined to clarify if and when there was a conceptualization of the cycle. Next an attempt is made to understand the changes the cycle underwent over time. Particular emphasis is laid on a defining element of the Passion cycle, that is, the way emotion is represented. This element is especially vivid in the Syro-Palestinian tradition and therefore its contribution and the insights it provides are assessed. The artistic evidence is viewed in parallel with the writings of Ephrem Syrus and Romanos the Melodist in order to thereby gain a full grasp of the importance of emotion to the formation of the Passion cycle. Answers to the question of how the expression of emotion may affect the viewer are gathered from descriptions, epigrams and homilies. Some general conclusions are that whereas fourth-century cycles concentrate on the triumphant message of redemption, which is rendered in a symbolic manner, subsequent cycles begin to focus on themes of suffering and to take on a more realistic, narrative form. The additions of scenes are, on the one hand, linked to the various theological issues of each time period and, on the other hand, to the viewer’s relationship to the image. Finally, the power of Passion images to move the beholder was of vital importance in remembering what Christ did for humanity.

citation: Daniel An, “Seeing Christ on the Cross in Late Antique Syria and Mesopotamia: Crosses, Crucifixes, and the Question of Iconicity,” Gesta 63:2 (2024): 95–120, https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1086/731244.

data.title: Seeing Christ on the Cross in Late Antique Syria and Mesopotamia: Crosses, Crucifixes, and the Question of Iconicity
data.abstractNote: This article begins with an account of cross-directed prayer from late antique Mesopotamia that describes seeing Christ on the cross. Using this passage as its frame, the article pursues two tracks. First, it examines the literary and material evidence for such seeing, drawing a distinction between the figuration of crosses (the degree of anthropomorphic imagery on their surfaces) and the iconicity of crosses (the degree to which viewers saw Christ’s body via physical crosses). It is argued that iconic descriptions of crosses in Syriac literature are more ambiguous than has hitherto been assumed, and that the documented material evidence for crosses in Syria and Mesopotamia indicates a general lack of figural imagery on crosses in the region. This raises the question, pursued in the second part of the article, of how social interactions between crosses and Syriac-speaking Christians may have contributed to their iconic status. Two brief case studies are presented, one following the movements of the processional cross during the eucharistic liturgy and the other examining physical interactions between monastics and crosses in their cells. Both case studies are used to advance the thesis that crosses functioned as social entities in some settings and that the social status of crosses as media of divine presence in turn shaped their iconic function as media through which Syriac-speaking Christians “saw” Christ’s body.

data.abstractNote: Addresses factors that evaluate the long-term prospects of a Christian presence in the regions of the Tur Abdin, south-eastern Turkey, as well as in Iraq. While Anschütz, also writing before the US invasion of Iraq, still had positive expectations for the Christian presence there, her analysis of the situation in the Tur Abdin is less promising. Restrictions regarding the exercise of Syriac language instruction for children, the discrimination of young men from the Syriac-speaking Christian community in military service, and repeated acts of forced expropriations of real estate property of Christians, as well as the gentrification of the Syrian-Christian population in the homeland and a desire on the part of Christians in the Tur Abdin to join family members who have reached a status of financial security in the West are key reasons that continue to contribute to the depopulation of the Christian landscape in south-eastern Turkey and to draw people to move westward. This tendency only intensifies a behavior that already characterizes the life of those who have gone into the diaspora. They suffer from a sense of loss of their roots and identity and they compensate for this by placing all their hopes in the acquisition of material goods.

data.title: Prolegomena to a Critical Edition of the Chronicle of Matthew of Edessa, with a Discussion of Computer-Aided Methods Used to Edit the Text
data.abstractNote: The Chronicle of Matthew of Edessa is the primary Armenian-language historical source for the eleventh and early twelfth centuries. Matthew was a monk who lived in the ethnically mixed city of Edessa; within his Chronicle, he describes the apogee of independent Armenia, its fall to piecemeal Byzantine annexation, the subsequent loss of Byzantium's eastern territory to the newcomer Saljuq Turks, and the sectarian tension that accompanied the First Crusade. This thesis sets out the methodology adopted for the construction of a critical edition of the text, addresses the approach that Matthew took to the composition of the Chronicle, and gives the edited text of the prophecies attributed to Yovhannēs Kozeṙn and the author's prologues to Books Two and Three of the Chronicle. Chapters 2 and 3 comprise a review of the scholarship to date on the Chronicle, and a discussion of the approach taken to a critical edition of the text. The Chronicle survives in a large number of relatively recently copied manuscripts; it was therefore necessary to devise an approach to text collation and editing that takes full advantage of recent advances in computational methods of philology. I have developed a set of software tools to assist in the task of editing the Chronicle; these tools are useful for the creation of text editions in any language that can be represented through the TEI XML standard. Chapters 4–8 give an examination of the overall framework of Matthew’s Chronicle, and of his interpretation of recent history within that framework. Following a long tradition of the use of prophecy to explain Armenian history, Matthew uses two prophecies attributed to the eleventh-century clerical scholar Yovhannēs Kozeṙn, themselves extended in the twelfth century under the influence of the Apocalypse attributed to Methodius, to frame his argument that both the Byzantine emperors and the Armenian kings had abandoned their responsibility toward the Armenian people. His attitude toward recent history, and particularly toward the Latins of Outremer, may be used to demonstrate that he wrote the Chronicle no later than 1137.
